name: empty-base-optimization
intent: Use C++'s empty-base layout rule to let an eligible stateless policy or mixin add no storage to its host, preserving zero-overhead composition while acknowledging that repeated or identity-sensitive subobjects, compiler ABI choices and C++20 member attributes determine whether the saving is available.
problem: A policy, allocator, comparator, hash functor, marker or interface mixin may carry only behavior, yet an ordinary empty object or data member still needs storage so distinct objects can have distinct addresses. Storing that helper as a member can add a byte and alignment padding to every host; inheriting it can avoid that cost only under EBO's distinct-type, non-virtual and layout rules, and the resulting layout is an ABI decision rather than a semantic guarantee.
context: C++ object-layout decisions inside a translation unit, library or binary: policy-based and mixin-heavy designs, allocator/deleter storage, iterator and view adaptors, and type-safe marker bases. It matters when objects are numerous or tightly packed (nodes, handles, entities), when a measured size budget justifies layout machinery, and when the toolchain and ABI boundary are under the author's control; C++20 [[no_unique_address]] is the member-based alternative.
benefits: Zero-cost composition when eligible: a stateless policy, allocator, comparator or marker can share the host's storage, so a canonical standard-layout Derived may remain sizeof(int) rather than paying for an empty member.

Keeps policy-based and mixin extension usable in performance-critical code: behavior is composed through bases instead of being hand-inlined or duplicated, with no runtime dispatch added by EBO itself.
Removes padding from repeated objects: avoiding a one-byte empty member and its alignment consequences can shrink arrays and container nodes, but the actual layout must be measured on the target ABI.

Lets library implementations compress stateless allocators, deleters and predicates behind a helper such as compressed_pair; the standard generally does not promise a particular sizeof for those library types.
No runtime cost when the representation is eligible: the saving is a compile-time layout choice, not an indirection, allocation or dispatch mechanism.
tradeoffs: Compiler and ABI dependence: MSVC documents a default multiple-inheritance layout that may leave padding between empty bases and offers __declspec(empty_bases); support and layout for [[no_unique_address]] also vary, so identical source can have different sizes on different toolchains.

ABI fragility: changing the set of empty bases, enabling an ABI layout switch, or replacing compressed storage with [[no_unique_address]] changes class layout and possibly subobject addresses; every object file, library and plugin using the type must agree.

Name leakage: inherited members and overloads can participate in lookup even with private inheritance because lookup precedes access checking; this can change overload resolution and ADL compared with a member-based helper.

The saving can disappear silently: a same-typed first data member, repeated inheritance from the same empty base, virtual inheritance, a final policy, a non-empty base, or a compiler's conservative layout can add storage without changing the source-level behavior.

Restructuring cost: state that naturally belongs in a member must not be moved into a base merely for size; constructor forwarding, initialization order, aggregate status and member-based encapsulation can all change. Use a compressed-pair helper when the policy should stay hidden.

Address identity is constrained, not erased: an empty base may share the complete object's address, but same-type subobjects still need distinct addresses; code using base addresses as identity or sentinels is invalid.

Debuggers, serializers and class-layout tools see bases that the author intended as pure implementation detail, and a member-based [[no_unique_address]] representation can change what those tools expose.

participants.responsibility: Carries only behavior - methods, typedefs and constants - such as a stateless allocator, comparator, hash policy, marker or interface mixin; it owns no data members, no virtual functions and no virtual bases, which makes zero-storage representation eligible but still target-layout dependent.
Inherits the empty base to obtain its behaviour and must not pay storage for it; owns the real state and forwards construction arguments to the base.
Optional library type that applies the optimization on the host's behalf, pairing one empty policy with one member so neither the policy's names nor the inheritance reach the host's interface.

use_cases: Allocator-aware containers: hold a possibly stateless allocator in a compressed pair so that a stateless allocator can add no bytes on the implementation (for example std::vector and other allocator-aware containers); do not infer the same layout for every standard-library type.
Policy-based design: a host class inherits several empty policy bases (comparator, hash, lock policy, logging policy) and must not pay bytes for the ones that carry no state.
Mixin markers: non-copyable, non-movable, interface-conformance or 'this type is a unit' markers applied to many small types.
Iterator and view adaptors wrapping one reference while inheriting an empty iterator-category or traits base.
Type-safe handles and strongly typed ids that store only the value and derive policy behaviour (formatting, validation, access rules) from a stateless base.
Packed data structures (node pools, entity tables, record arrays) where one byte of padding per element multiplies into megabytes.

std::unique_ptr deleter storage: libc++ and MSVC implementations use tuple/compressed-pair-like helpers to store the pointer with a deleter; an eligible stateless deleter can be free in that implementation, but the C++ standard does not require unique_ptr to be exactly pointer-sized.

Standard-library implementation internals: containers and callable wrappers may compress stateless allocators, comparators or deleters, but their representation and sizeof are implementation details; use the library contract rather than depending on a particular helper type.
CRTP stateless mixins: a templated mixin that contributes methods and no state can exploit EBO, provided each base is eligible and distinct; repeated or stateful mixins still consume storage.

Tuple-like and range-adaptor storage: implementations commonly use empty leaf bases or equivalent compressed elements for tag, predicate and policy objects, but the optimization is not a portable promise for every tuple or adaptor.

std::optional and std::variant layout: an implementation may reuse tail padding or compress empty alternatives, but engaged-state and discriminator storage are observable only through the library's semantics, not a portable sizeof guarantee.

Custom deleters for resource handles (FILE*, HANDLE, sqlite3*): a compressed-pair or [[no_unique_address]] member can keep a stateless deleter out of the handle's footprint on an implementation that supports it; assert the size instead of assuming it equals the raw pointer.

libc++ compressed storage: LLVM's libc++ 20 release notes document replacing internal __compressed_pair with [[no_unique_address]] to reduce compile and debug-information size, while warning that object layout and ABI can change.

Boost compressed_pair: Boost.Utility explicitly applies EBO when either pair element is an empty class, giving a reusable library carrier when a policy must remain behind accessors rather than leak through the host's inheritance.

Policy-heavy generic types: a C++20 [[no_unique_address]] member can compress several empty hash, predicate and allocator policies while keeping them members; the WG21 P0840 example uses exactly this layout for a hash_map-like type.

Packed data structures (node pools, entity tables, record arrays) where one byte or an alignment word per element multiplies into megabytes; use measured layouts and preserve the same-type address rule.

MSVC ABI migration: a library that opts into __declspec(empty_bases) can remove padding between empty bases, but Microsoft documents the switch as an ABI change that requires rebuilding every client using the affected type.
avoid_when: You are on C++20 or later and the helper is genuinely a member: [[no_unique_address]] expresses potentially-overlapping member storage without inheritance, name leakage or hierarchy changes, subject to compiler support and address-identity caveats.

The language already provides a stateless behavior carrier (Java/C#/Swift/Kotlin/Scala interfaces and protocol extensions, Python/Ruby/JavaScript mixins, Rust ZSTs, Go zero-size structs) - use that model instead of importing a C++ layout trick.

The base is likely to gain state later: any data member, virtual function, virtual base or final marker cancels eligibility or changes layout, so use ordinary composition until the representation is stable.

The objects cross an ABI boundary you do not control (prebuilt third-party libraries, stable plugin interfaces), because changing EBO, compressed-pair or [[no_unique_address]] layout forces all users to recompile.
The saving is immaterial - a handful of long-lived objects - and keeping a plain member leaves the code more obvious and avoids address/lookup surprises.

You need a portable sizeof promise for a standard-library type: implementations may compress empty policies differently, so use a measured, versioned wrapper or accept the specified layout rather than depending on EBO.
anti_patterns: Naive EBCO refactoring: move an empty data member into public or protected inheritance -> names, conversions and overload lookup leak into the host -> instead use private inheritance or a compressed/member helper when the relationship is not semantic.

Repeated inheritance from the same empty base (for example boost::noncopyable reached through several paths): same-type subobjects need distinct addresses -> the type still costs bytes or violates layout assumptions -> instead use one base or distinct wrapper types with deliberate semantics.

Deriving from an 'empty' base that has virtual functions or a virtual destructor -> the vptr makes it non-empty and base deletion semantics change -> instead use a non-virtual, stateless carrier or an explicit owning interface.

Relying on the address of an empty base subobject for identity, tagging or sentinel values -> legal overlap and same-type address rules make the identity unstable -> instead use an explicit tag or state field.

Enabling __declspec(empty_bases) or adding an empty base across a library boundary -> independently compiled objects disagree about offsets and subobject addresses -> instead version the ABI and rebuild every user of the class.

Treating [[no_unique_address]] as a universal zero-size guarantee -> same-type members, overalignment and implementation choices can still add bytes or alter identity -> instead document it as potentially overlapping storage and test each supported ABI.
design_principles: Zero-overhead abstraction: behaviour that carries no state must not consume object size.
Object identity is a layout force: distinct objects of the same type need distinct addresses, and EBO is the language's sanctioned exception rather than a general licence for zero-sized types.
Encapsulate the layout trick: compress one empty policy with one member behind a small helper (compressed pair) instead of exposing bases on the public type.
Prefer composition over inheritance, except where inheritance is exactly what buys the layout - private, stateless and first.
Keep policy bases interface-only: any mixin that owns state should own it in the host class, not in the base.
best_practices: static_assert the expected size (for example sizeof(Derived) == sizeof(int)) so the optimization is a tested property rather than an assumption, and keep a per-ABI expectation when compilers differ.

Inherit the empty base privately and place it first when inheritance is the chosen representation: private inheritance minimizes name leakage, while first position makes the intended layout easier to inspect.
Keep the base genuinely empty - no data members, no virtual functions, no virtual bases, no repeated inheritance from the same type.
Prefer [[no_unique_address]] (or a compressed-pair helper) in C++20 and later when the policy is conceptually a member, so the host keeps a member-based interface without inherited names.
Give any publicly exposed empty base a protected non-virtual destructor so that deleting through a base pointer is a compile error.
Treat every change to the set of empty bases or compression attributes as an ABI change: bump the library version and recompile all users.

Gate EBO eligibility with std::is_empty_v<T> && !std::is_final_v<T>, then verify the resulting layout; the guard selects a compressed-pair or member specialization but cannot make every ABI choose the same size.

Prefer [[no_unique_address]] (C++20) over inheritance when the policy is genuinely a member: it avoids is-a semantics, works with final types, and makes the zero-cost intent explicit; fall back to compressed-pair inheritance for C++17 and earlier.

Follow the target MSVC EBCO documentation and vendor-supported attributes rather than assuming /Zc:ebo or a standard attribute spelling has identical behavior across toolsets; static_assert the layout on every supported toolchain.

Watch the first-member rule: EBO is prohibited when the same type appears as both a base and the first non-static data member, because the compiler must give those same-type subobjects distinct addresses.
Handle alignment cascades: multiple empty bases can still induce padding before a stricter-aligned member; static_assert the actual size on each supported ABI.
Avoid virtual inheritance with EBO: virtual bases and their metadata are not the zero-storage policy representation; prefer non-virtual inheritance or an attributed member.
Solve repeated-inheritance address identity only with distinct wrapper types when separate subobjects are semantically valid; do not use a wrapper to hide accidental duplicate policy state.
Use [[no_unique_address]] on ordinary data members, not as a claim that union members or complete objects have zero size; document that an attributed member may share an address.

Verify EBO with static_assert(sizeof(Derived) == sizeof(expected_field)) in every ABI configuration that first sees the class: the rule is constrained by layout requirements, and a compiler flag or later base change can still alter size.
Test EBO eligibility with std::is_empty_v<T> in templates and provide a non-EBO fallback for non-empty/final policies, so a size regression is explicit rather than accidental.
Do not treat a C++ empty class as a general zero-sized type: complete objects and array elements still need storage, unlike Rust ZSTs or Go zero-size structs.
Keep layout-sensitive assertions and compiler-specific attributes out of stable public ABI unless the supported toolchain matrix is part of the contract.
sources: Boost.Utility compressed_pair documentation - applies EBO when either template argument is an empty class and provides accessors that hide the inheritance helper: https://www.boost.org/latest/libs/utility/doc/html/utility/utilities/compressed_pair.html
Alexandrescu, A. Modern C++ Design: Generic Programming and Design Patterns Applied. Addison-Wesley, 2001 - policy-based design and the compressed-pair storage trick for stateless policies.
cppreference std::unique_ptr - specifies the deleter template parameter without promising a pointer-sized representation: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/unique_ptr

Scott Meyers, Effective C++ Third Edition, Item 39 'Use private inheritance judiciously' - covers EBO as a reason private inheritance can beat composition when an empty base must be stored at zero cost.
Scott Meyers, Effective C++ Third Edition, Item 40 'Use multiple inheritance judiciously' - warns that multiple inheritance and virtual bases complicate layout and object-size reasoning.

P0840R2, 'Language support for empty objects' - proposal text on potentially-overlapping [[no_unique_address]] members, same-type address limits and policy storage: https://open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/papers/2018/p0840r2.html
Microsoft Learn, empty_bases - documents EBCO, multiple-inheritance padding and the ABI-breaking rebuild requirement: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/cpp/empty-bases?view=msvc-170
C++ Stories, 'Empty Base Class Optimisation, no_unique_address and unique_ptr' - practical implementation comparison and portability cautions: https://www.cppstories.com/2021/no-unique-address/
Aleksey Shipilev, 'Java Objects Inside Out' - measured HotSpot object headers and the non-portable nature of runtime layout claims: https://shipilev.net/jvm/objects-inside-out/

Optimizing the Layout of Empty Base Classes in VS2015 Update 2 - Microsoft documents __declspec(empty_bases), padding in multiple inheritance and the ABI cost of changing layout: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/optimizing-the-layout-of-empty-base-classes-in-vs2015-update-2-3/

LLVM libc++ 20 release notes - replacing internal __compressed_pair with [[no_unique_address]], with compile/debug-size benefits and ABI effects: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/libcxx/docs/ReleaseNotes/20.rst

LLVM libc++ compressed-pair header - legacy ABI compatibility helper versus _LIBCPP_NO_UNIQUE_ADDRESS for new structures: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/llvm/llvm-project/main/libcxx/include/__memory/compressed_pair.h
Boost.Utility compressed_pair documentation - applies EBO when either template argument is an empty class: https://www.boost.org/latest/libs/utility/doc/html/utility/utilities/compressed_pair.html

P0840R2, 'Language support for empty objects' - proposal text defining potentially-overlapping [[no_unique_address]] members, same-type address limits and the hash_map policy example: https://open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/papers/2018/p0840r2.html

Empty Base Class Optimisation, no_unique_address and unique_ptr (C++ Stories, 2021) - practical implementation comparison with Microsoft STL and compressed-pair examples: https://www.cppstories.com/2021/no-unique-address/
